NVS, IONS, AMGN Stocks Drop After-Hours — What’s Driving The Selloff?
sum: Shares of Novartis (NVS) sank after-hours on Friday after a closely watched heart-disease trial failed to show that lowering a stubborn inherited risk factor actually prevented heart attacks and strokes.

U.S.-listed Novartis stock (NVS) closed at $159.99, then slipped as much as about 7% in after-hours trading. Partner Ionis Pharmaceuticals (IONS), which licensed the drug, also fell roughly 10% after the close.

The late-stage Lp(a)HORIZON study tested pelacarsen in 8,323 people who already had cardiovascular disease and high lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a)—a genetically driven blood fat that diet and lifestyle barely change. About one in five people worldwide have elevated Lp(a), and there is still no approved medicine that targets it.

Pelacarsen did what it was designed to do: it lowered Lp(a). It did not, however, cut the combined risk of cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, or urgent procedures to open a blocked heart artery versus placebo. Patients were already on standard treatments such as cholesterol and blood-pressure medicines. Full results will be presented at a medical meeting, the company said.

“These are not the results we hoped for,” said Shreeram Aradhye, Novartis’s chief medical officer, adding that the data still help scientists understand whether cutting Lp(a) reduces leftover heart risk when other factors are already controlled.

Pelacarsen had been one of the company’s biggest late-stage bets in heart disease. The miss removes a potential growth engine just as Novartis works to replace older blockbusters facing generic competition.

The pipeline is not empty. Days earlier, Novartis’s remibrutinib succeeded in two large multiple-sclerosis trials, lifting shares. Other late-stage programs, including ianalumab in autoimmune disease and radioligand cancer drugs, remain on the calendar.

Amgen stock: Dazodalibep meets both Phase 3 Sjogren's endpoints
sum: Amgen announced positive Phase 3 results for its investigational treatment dazodalibep on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. In the randomized OASIZ-301 study, both tested dosing regimens met the primary endpoint after 48 weeks, according to the Amgen investor release.

OASIZ-301 enrolled 648 patients with moderate-to-severe systemic disease activity. The mean baseline score on the ESSDAI measure was 10.2, with the primary endpoint defined as the change from baseline after 48 weeks.

The 1,500-milligram regimen given every four weeks produced a least-squares mean ESSDAI reduction of 5.6 points, compared with 3.8 points for placebo. The placebo-adjusted difference was 1.8 points, with an adjusted p-value below 0.001. The 3,000-milligram regimen administered every 12 weeks reduced ESSDAI by 5.2 points, versus 3.8 points for placebo. Its placebo-adjusted difference was 1.4 points, with an adjusted p-value of 0.010.

Amgen said treatment effects appeared as early as Week 4 and continued through Week 48. The company described the findings as support for dazodalibep's potential as a first-in-class CD40L antagonist fusion protein, but the treatment remains investigational and is not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

The four-week regimen also improved patient-reported dryness, a key symptom of Sjogren's disease. Compared with placebo, the regimen delivered placebo-adjusted improvements of 1.17 points on the dryness domain of the ESSPRI scale and 0.93 points on the DASPRI dryness domain. Both comparisons had adjusted p-values below 0.001.

Additional analyses favored dazodalibep on total ESSPRI and DASPRI scores, with mean improvement in total ESSPRI exceeding 1.5 points for both dosing regimens. Amgen also reported greater increases in stimulated salivary flow and higher proportions of patients meeting STAR response criteria, a composite measure covering patient-reported symptoms and objective disease activity.

The most common adverse events occurring more frequently with dazodalibep than placebo included nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infections, hypertension and infusion-related reactions. Amgen said these events were generally mild to moderate.

Amgen (AMGN) sits in a peer group of six drugmakers with Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Merck, Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb. Over its latest four fiscal quarters, Amgen ranked second of the six on both revenue growth and operating margin. Yet its P/E ranks only third of the four companies with a comparable one, counting from the highest. How much less are you paying for Amgen's profit than for Johnson & Johnson's?

Investors pay 27.0 times Amgen's earnings over its latest four fiscal quarters, compared with 42.0 times for Johnson & Johnson over its own. During that time, Amgen grew revenue 8.2%, finishing slightly ahead of the 7.8% managed by Johnson & Johnson. Amgen recorded a 32.4% operating margin, against 25.7% for Johnson & Johnson, leaving Amgen with more of each sales dollar as operating profit. Industry classifications group Johnson & Johnson as a pharmaceuticals company and Amgen as a biotechnology one, so part of that margin gap may come from the kind of business each runs.

AbbVie is the only peer that grew faster than Amgen, at 10.7%, and investors pay more for it, at 50.5 times earnings. Bristol Myers Squibb trades at 13.9 times earnings, but its revenue grew just 4.2%. Because Merck and Pfizer each reported a loss in at least one of their latest four quarters, their P/Es are not comparable. Amgen's discount to Johnson & Johnson does not come with weaker growth or a thinner margin.

In the third quarter of 2026, six medicines that management counts as its main growth drivers generated more than 70% of Amgen's product sales. The group collectively grew 27% from a year earlier, management said on the November 3, 2026 call, outpacing the 8% growth in total product sales. Repatha, a cholesterol-lowering drug, recorded $1.1 billion in quarterly sales, up 37%. EVENITY, used in osteoporosis, rose 39% to $751 million.

Amgen stock heads into ACR week with dazodalibep update
sum: Amgen is heading into a closely watched week of clinical presentations as the American College of Rheumatology Convergence takes place from November 8 through November 11, 2026. The most important appointment for investors is a late-breaking presentation on Wednesday, November 11, covering Phase 3 OASIZ-301 results for dazodalibep in adults with Sjogren's disease and moderate-to-severe systemic disease activity.

In an Amgen investor-relations release dated October 27, the company said the trial met its primary endpoint. At Week 48, disease activity fell by a least-squares mean of 5.6 points with dazodalibep dosed every four weeks and by 5.2 points with dosing every 12 weeks, compared with a 3.8-point reduction for placebo.

The placebo-adjusted improvements were 1.8 points for the four-week regimen and 1.4 points for the 12-week regimen. Amgen said both results were statistically significant, with adjusted p-values below 0.001 and 0.010, respectively. The treatment effect appeared as early as Week 4 and continued through the end of the 48-week study.

Dazodalibep also improved patient-reported dryness in the four-week dosing group. The ESSPRI dryness score declined by 2.50 points from baseline, compared with 1.33 points for placebo, while the DASPRI dryness score fell by 1.98 points versus 1.05 points for placebo. Amgen reported similar rates of treatment-emergent adverse events, serious adverse events and discontinuations across the treatment groups.

The company is positioning dazodalibep as a potential first-in-class CD40L antagonist. The investigational medicine is designed to disrupt interactions among T cells, glandular epithelial cells, B cells and other antigen-presenting cells. Amgen said there are currently no FDA-approved medicines for Sjogren's disease, leaving regulatory and clinical execution as key hurdles before any commercial opportunity can be assessed.

The November 11 presentation will provide a fuller examination of the OASIZ-301 findings. Investors are also waiting for OASIZ-303, a separate Phase 3 study in patients with high symptom burden and lower systemic disease activity.

Amgen (AMGN) stock returned 59.4% over the past year, against 9.9% for the S&P 500. The shares also cost more per dollar of earnings than the index, suggesting that buyers expect the company’s growth to continue. Part of that expansion comes from biosimilars, which are Amgen’s versions of drugs such as EYLEA, and the company has more of them in development. On a November 3 call, management outlined what it will take for those upcoming launches to succeed. What could go wrong for Amgen’s next biosimilars?

The risk is that Amgen’s next biosimilars reach the market after the first wave of competing products, and it remains too early to know whether they will. During the November 3 call, management said Amgen aims to be first or in the first wave with its biosimilar launches. Executives called this timing “really important to establish a decent competitive position,” adding that management believes Amgen is in that position.

The next four pipeline drugs are versions of EYLEA HD, OPDIVO, KEYTRUDA and OCREVUS, which management called large market opportunities. Because all four are still in late-stage clinical development, an early launch is management’s belief, not a result.

Biosimilars generated $977 million in fiscal Q3 2026, accounting for about 9% of Amgen’s total revenue. While they remain a small part of the company, these sales are growing rapidly. Biosimilar sales rose 26% from a year earlier, compared with an 8% increase for all of Amgen’s product sales. PAVBLU, Amgen’s version of EYLEA, made up $300 million of that total, climbing 41% from a year earlier.

The stock price leaves little room for disappointment. Amgen closed on November 5 just 3.8% below its highest close of the past year. The stock trades at 26.5 times earnings, against 22.9 for the S&P 500.

Is Amgen Stock Worth More Than Its Competitors?
sum: Amgen (AMGN) competes in a tight peer group of six large drugmakers alongside AbbVie, Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Pfizer, and Bristol-Myers Squibb. The company ranks second within this group for both sales growth and operating margin. Its valuation tells a different story. Leaving out Merck and Pfizer, which each reported a loss in at least one of their last four quarters, Amgen has the third highest P/E of the four companies that can be compared. So how far apart are what Amgen delivers and what you pay for it?

Johnson & Johnson provides the clearest point of comparison. Amgen grew its revenue by 9.1% over the past twelve months, beating the 8.1% rate at Johnson & Johnson. Amgen also retained a larger share of its sales as operating profit, posting a margin of 30.0% against Johnson & Johnson’s 26.8%. Yet investors pay just 25.8 times earnings for Amgen, compared to 30.2 times for Johnson & Johnson.

AbbVie is the sole peer to beat Amgen on both growth and margin. That performance comes at a steep premium, with AbbVie trading at 78.8 times earnings. Bristol-Myers Squibb offers the lowest valuation at 12.7 times, but its revenue grew by a modest 3.1%. Merck and Pfizer fall out of the price ranking entirely. Both of those companies reported a loss in at least one of their last four quarters.

Executives point to six key growth drivers for Amgen. The company reported on its fiscal Q2 2026 call, held August 4, 2026, that these six grew 26% from a year earlier. Together they accounted for nearly 70% of product sales in that quarter. Repatha, which lowers LDL cholesterol, saw its sales rise 37% in the quarter.

Two other drugs are pulling the overall numbers in the opposite direction. Combined sales of Prolia and XGEVA fell 33% in the same quarter. Management noted that biosimilar competitors, rival copies of the two drugs, have now launched.

Overall growth at Amgen has slowed. Revenue growth hit 16.4% two years ago and 12.9% a year ago, before slowing again over the latest twelve months. The market price appears to assume this slowdown continues.
Amgen expects 2026 revenue of $38.2 billion to $39.4 billion, according to statements management made on that August call. That guidance represents a raise.

The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke and urgent coronary revascularization requiring hospitalization.

sum: A pair of phase 3 psoriasis studies of Alumis’ TYK2 inhibitor have hit their primary endpoints, setting the biotech up to file for approval of a potential challenger to Bristol Myers Squibb’s Sotyktu. With the news, Alumis’ shares more than doubled in premarket trading.

The biotech tested its TYK2 inhibitor, envudeucitinib, in two studies that collectively enrolled more than 1,700 adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis. About half of the participants received Alumis’ oral drug candidate twice daily. The other half of the patients were split up to receive either apremilast, which Amgen sells as Otezla, or placebo.

On average across the two trials, 74% of people on envudeucitinib experienced at least a 75% improvement in their symptoms, as measured on the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI), at Week 16. Alumis said 59% of patients scored zero or one on the static Physician’s Global Assessment (sPGA) at Week 16. The PASI 75 and sPGA results met the trials’ co-primary endpoints.

At Week 24, 65% of patients experienced at least a 90% improvement on the PASI. Alumis reported “clear separation from placebo” on PASI 90 as early as Week 4. More than 40% of patients met the PASI 100 criteria by Week 24, indicating that they had completely clear skin. Alumis also said it saw clinically meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes related to quality of life and itch.

BMS reported PASI 75 response rates of 53% and 58% at Week 16 in the phase 3 trials quoted (PDF) on the Sotyktu label. At Week 24, the proportion of patients achieving PASI 90 on Sotyktu ranged from 32% to 42%. BMS reported PASI 100 results in 10% to 14% of patients in the two Sotyktu studies.

With the caveat that cross-trial comparisons can be unreliable, the results appear to favor Alumis' envudeucitinib over Sotyktu. The envudeucitinib results look to be in line with the expectations Alumis CEO Martin Babler set at an investor event in September.

Noting that Alumis saw a 64% placebo-adjusted PASI 75 at Week 12 of a phase 2 trial, Babler said a result in the 50% to 60% range at Week 16 would be competitive. Alumis’ phase 3 release lacks results from the placebo arm. Between 9% and 13% of patients on placebo in BMS’ Sotyktu trials met the PASI 75 criteria at Week 16.

items.t: FBI accuses Forbes-celebrated Nigerian tech boss, Izunna Okonkwo, of $41 million bank fraud, money laundering
sum: The FBI has identified Izunna Okonkwo, a celebrated Pastel tech startup co-founder who made the highly coveted Forbes 30-under-30 list in 2023, as a person of interest and co-conspirator in an insider trading and money laundering scheme that generated $41 million in illegal profit from several companies within five years, court filings reviewed by Peoples Gazette showed.

Mr Okonkwo, who took graduate studies at Stanford University, was buying stocks and securities based on the material non-public information shared by investment banker Gyunho Justin Kim with his American-Pakistani friend, Saad Shoukat.

Messrs Kim and Shoukat were good friends who met in 2018 while interning at different multinational establishments. The friendship devolved into criminal activity as Mr Kim shared crucial MNPI about upcoming acquisitions with Mr Shoukat, who then tipped Mr Okonkwo and other co-conspirators. The Nigerian and Pakistani were friends who met in college.
Mr Okonkwo, 30, knew Mr Kim was the source of the illicit gains and eventually suggested facilitating a new employment for him after years of raking in millions from the tip-offs.

Mr Kim worked at Citibank Investment Group’s division in San Francisco and was privy to confidential financial intelligence, as Citibank often acted as a middleman, providing financial advisory when negotiations for company acquisitions began.

“Okonkwo knew that KIM worked at the Investment Bank, and Saad Shoukat and Okonkwo communicated on an encrypted messaging app about the impending Reata deal before it was public,” FBI Special Agent Antony Belitti wrote in a complaint to the U.S. District Court for New Jersey on November 24. “Saad Shoukat exchanged messages with Okonkwo about helping Kim find a new job.”

Mr Shoukat brokered a deal with Mr Okonkwo to use his brokerage accounts to trade. The deal would fetch the Nigerian tech boss 50 per cent of all ill-gotten proceeds. Mr Okonkwo also cultivated his own personal relationship with the Citibank snitch to secure continued access to insider information.
